beats.say: Agentrix. Upgrade your website into WebAgents. This is our entry for Challenge 1, Blast Radius Zero.

About two in five websites run on WordPress. For a small business, that often means a site that waits. Questions go unanswered at night, plugins go unpatched, and some sites are quietly hacked. Move one the usual way, and you copy the hack across.
This is agentrix.website. You paste your site's address, and the site's own guide walks you through what happens next.

badge: Assess on Zavora's infected test site
beats.say: A real Firefox reads the old site from a sealed room on a separate Vultr VM. The room holds no keys, and it can reach only this site. Watch the receipt. This page tried to send our browser to Vultr's metadata address. Refused, and written down. Then the honest report: hidden spam links, a disguised miner script, and text aimed at AI agents, each with its evidence.

Vultr is the whole stack. A control VM plans the work and signs every job. A separate VX1 sandbox VM runs each job in its own gVisor room, with no secrets and no public inbound. Every model call goes to Vultr Serverless Inference, through one gateway that holds the only key.
Every job is a signed spec going in, and a signed receipt coming out: what ran, what it touched, what was refused, and proof that the room was destroyed.

beats.speed_label: 4x speed. The Move page shows real time
beats.say: Now the Move. The old WordPress runs from its own database in a sealed room, with no route out. Its code tries to phone home. That fails, and lands on the receipt. Everything infected is quarantined, with the reason in plain words. A Vultr model writes the new pages, a room with no network renders them, and a Vultr vision model checks each one against the old site.
Nothing goes live until the owner says so. My passkey signs this exact card. The new site is live, the old one is kept, and undo lasts thirty days.

Here is one room's receipt: gVisor, a read-only root, caps on memory and processes, and destroyed: true. Ten attacks are planted in this test site, including a fork bomb and a webshell, and the gauntlet scores them from receipts.
Each Vultr model has one job, and something checks its work. Qwen builds the pages, DeepSeek checks them by eye, Nemotron screens for instructions aimed at AI, and systemone scores the risk.
The new site answers visitors from its own pages, with citations, and says when it doesn't know.

Customers' AI agents get a door of their own. In our race on Sunday morning, an agent ordered a cake through the new site's door in under eight seconds. On the old site, it gave up after twenty-two steps.
Every morning, the owner gets a brief and a short list of decisions, each one a tap and a passkey.
Moving is free. Plans start at twenty-nine dollars a month, paid with PayPal, and agencies pay per site. Every site moved is steady Vultr compute, storage and inference.
We read all ninety-three entries before ours. Containment is table stakes. None of them moves a business.
